title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #921**

For k ≥ 4, what is f_k(n) = largest m such that an n-vertex k-chromatic graph can have all odd cycles of length > m?

**Answer: SOLVED**

f_k(n) ≍ n^{1/(k-2)} by Kierstead-Szemerédi-Trotter (1984).

This completely characterizes the trade-off between chromatic number and odd cycle length.
mathContext: A foundational result in extremal graph theory connecting local structure (cycles) to global properties (coloring).

title: Simple Graph Structure
content:
**Graph V:**

A simple graph on vertex type V consists of:
- adj : V → V → Prop (adjacency relation)
- symm : adjacency is symmetric
- loopless : no vertex is adjacent to itself

This matches the standard mathematical definition of an undirected simple graph.
mathContext: Simple graphs are the foundation of graph theory. No loops, no multiple edges.

title: Chromatic Number
content:
**chromaticNumber χ(G):**

The minimum k such that G has a proper k-coloring - assigning colors 1,...,k to vertices so adjacent vertices get different colors.

**Key Facts:**
- χ(G) = 1 iff G has no edges
- χ(G) = 2 iff G is bipartite (no odd cycles)
- χ(G) ≥ 3 requires at least one odd cycle

Axiomatized because the full definition requires Fintype and decidability infrastructure.
mathContext: The chromatic number is one of the most fundamental graph invariants, central to the Four Color Theorem.

title: Odd Girth
content:
**oddGirth:**

The length of the shortest odd cycle in G, or 0 if G is bipartite (has no odd cycles).

**Examples:**
- Complete graph K_n: odd girth = 3 (has triangles)
- Cycle C_5: odd girth = 5
- Cycle C_6: odd girth = 0 (bipartite)

Axiomatized to avoid the complexity of cycle enumeration in the formalization.
mathContext: Odd girth generalizes the classical girth (shortest cycle) by focusing only on odd-length cycles.

title: The Function f_k(n) and Well-Definedness
content:
**f(k, n):**

The largest m such that there exists an n-vertex graph with χ = k and odd girth > m.

Equivalently: f_k(n) = max{oddGirth(G) - 1 : G has n vertices and χ(G) = k}

The well-definedness axiom guarantees f(k,n) ≥ 1 for k ≥ 4 and n ≥ k, meaning k-chromatic graphs with positive odd girth always exist.
mathContext: This extremal function captures the fundamental trade-off between chromatic number and odd cycle structure.

title: Erdős-Gallai Conjecture and KST Resolution
content:
**erdos_gallai_conjecture(k) and kierstead_szemeredi_trotter:**

The conjecture states: for k ≥ 4, f_k(n) ≍ n^{1/(k-2)}.

The notation ≍ means asymptotically equivalent:
∃ c₁, c₂ > 0: c₁ · n^{1/(k-2)} ≤ f_k(n) ≤ c₂ · n^{1/(k-2)}

The KST axiom asserts this conjecture is proved for all k ≥ 4. The proof required combining regularity methods (Szemerédi), coloring theory (Kierstead), and combinatorial geometry (Trotter).
mathContext: Asymptotic notation captures the essential growth behavior up to constant factors, standard in extremal combinatorics.

title: The k = 4 Case: Gallai + Erdős
content:
**gallai_lower_bound, erdos_upper_bound, and k4_case:**

Gallai (1963) proved f_4(n) ≥ c√n by constructing explicit 4-chromatic graphs with large odd girth. Erdős proved the matching upper bound f_4(n) ≤ C√n (unpublished).

The k4_case theorem combines both bounds constructively:
∃ c₁, c₂ > 0: c₁√n ≤ f_4(n) ≤ c₂√n

Note: 1/(k-2) = 1/2 when k = 4, matching √n = n^{1/2}. This case provided key intuition for the general exponent formula.
mathContext: The k = 4 case was resolved before the general conjecture and is the only case with a constructive proof in this formalization.

title: General Lower and Upper Bounds
mathContext: Lower bounds require constructing extremal examples; upper bounds use the regularity lemma, one of the most powerful tools in combinatorics.

title: Final Status: Problem Solved
content:
**erdos_921_status:**

∀ k ≥ 4, erdos_gallai_conjecture k

This states that for all k ≥ 4, the conjecture f_k(n) ≍ n^{1/(k-2)} is proved. The proof follows directly from the kierstead_szemeredi_trotter axiom.

The problem stood for over 20 years between Gallai's partial result (1963) and the full resolution by KST (1984). It remains an important result in understanding how local structure (odd cycles) constrains global properties (chromatic number).
mathContext: This theorem summarizes the complete resolution of Erdős Problem #921.
